job.style: a diary entry or letter by a student

response.passage: Dear Diary, today in history class, we discussed why the Industrial Revolution didn't instantly erase manual work. My teacher explained that many Victorian industrialists actually preferred hand labour over machines. This wasn't because machines were low quality, but because machines couldn't produce the intricate, irregular designs that wealthy aristocrats demanded. Furthermore, the steam engine was expensive and prone to breaking down, so it didn't immediately replace all human workers as some might assume. We also looked at why Indian textiles declined. It wasn't because Indian weavers lacked skill or refused to use new technology. Instead, the British government imposed heavy import duties on Indian cloth while flooding our markets with cheap, mass-produced British goods. This systematic policy crippled our local weavers, who were actually world-renowned for their superior quality. It is a common myth that our textiles vanished because they were inferior; in reality, they were victims of unfair colonial trade policies that prioritized British factory profits over our centuries-old craft traditions.
response.summary: Industrialists often preferred hand labour for its unique designs rather than machine efficiency. The decline of Indian textiles was caused by unfair British trade policies rather than the poor quality of Indian goods.
